questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A doctor's note on one street
questions.learningObjective: Identify the shared environmental source behind a street-level outbreak
questions.stem: Your waterworks redesign brief notes that eleven households on one terraced street fell ill with fever within a single fortnight. What does this pattern most directly indicate?

options.text: Cases clustered by household around a shared water source rather than a shared food
The street's houses were older and less well built than those on the next terrace
options.misconception: assumes building age alone explains the outbreak

options.text: The households had all recently moved there from one rural district
options.misconception: blames shared migration instead of shared services

options.text: Doctors were counting cases more carefully on this street than elsewhere in town
options.misconception: treats better case counting as a cause of illness

questions.explanation: Cases clustering by household across one street point to a shared source, usually the well or pump. Building age, migration and counting effort do not explain why only that street was hit.
questions.hint: Look for what every affected household shared.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonial economy built on one export
questions.learningObjective: Explain how dependence on one export made a colonial economy fragile
questions.stem: Draft a note for the works council on why a colony that exported only one crop suffered sharp downturns whenever world prices fell.

answer.exemplar: A strong answer argues that a single-export colony had no second industry to absorb workers or capital when the export price fell. Land, credit and wages were all tied to that commodity, so a price decline cut incomes, tax receipts and land values together, and no alternative sector existed to cushion the shock.

questions.explanation: A single-export economy concentrates risk: a price fall cuts wages, land values and tax receipts together. A good answer makes that linkage and notes no other industry could absorb freed labour.
questions.hint: Ask what else the colony could produce.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colony's trade return
questions.learningObjective: Read a colonial customs return for evidence of a trade deficit

stimulus.body: The 1889 customs return lists 418,000 sacks of coffee exported, 3,200 sacks of woven cloth imported and 900 barrels of whale oil sent abroad. Exports are valued at 1,240,000 pounds sterling and imports at 1,410,000.

questions.stem: Your harbour works brief cites the 1889 customs return above. What does it show about the colony's trade position?

options.text: The colony nearly balanced its trade, since exports and imports differed by only 17 percent
options.misconception: treats a modest trade gap as roughly balanced

options.text: The colony sold its whale oil at home, so woven cloth had no place in the return
options.misconception: confuses a listed export with a domestic sale

options.text: Exports did not cover imports, so the gap had to be financed from outside the colony
The large coffee volume shows the colony was spreading risk across several export lines
options.misconception: reads one large export as broad diversification

questions.explanation: Exports of 1.24 million pounds against imports of 1.41 million left a 170,000 pound deficit. A colony cannot settle that gap with goods it does not produce, so it must be financed from abroad.
questions.hint: Compare the two totals in the return.

options.misconception: reads food imports as evidence of dietary improvement

options.misconception: confuses a downstream benefit with upstream priority rights

options.text: Land once used for food crops was converted to one export crop, narrowing local subsistence

questions.explanation: The notice shows food plots falling from 400 to 90 hectares while a single export crop took 62 percent of cultivable land. That conversion, not soil exhaustion or mill privileges, is the change in land use.

options.text: Rights to drill, extract and sell the oil, while the state kept sovereignty and most taxes
Full ownership of the field and its revenue, handed over in exchange for a state loan
options.misconception: reads a concession as a transfer of ownership

options.text: Only the right to explore, with all drilling reserved to the state's own engineers
options.misconception: confuses exploration rights with production rights

options.text: A fixed price for oil for thirty years in return for a guaranteed annual payment
options.misconception: assumes the concession was a price fixing contract

questions.stem: While drafting the access agreement for a pipeline, you read a clause requiring the holder to ship 60 percent of its output on government vessels at rates set by the state. What does the clause do?

options.text: It guarantees the state a steady profit from every barrel the company lifts
options.misconception: assumes a shipping clause fixes the selling price

options.text: It limits the company's freedom to choose buyers and carriers for most of its output
It transfers the concession itself to the state once the term of the agreement ends
options.misconception: reads a shipping clause as a reversion of ownership

answer.exemplar: A good answer argues that burning coal filled the air with soot and smoke that settled on buildings, blackened laundry and damaged vegetation, and that in narrow streets the smoke could not disperse. questions.explanation: Coal smoke in narrow streets reduced light, dirtied surfaces and made breathing difficult. A good answer links soot to complaint and to the emergence of smoke rules as nuisance control.

questions.stem: Write a short note for a port engineer explaining what a customs return can and cannot tell you about the traffic a port will have to handle.

answer.exemplar: A good answer explains that the return shows values and volumes by commodity, which lets an engineer separate bulk traffic from high-value cargo and see whether the mix is raw or finished. It also notes the limits: values move with prices, small voyages go unrecorded, and the return gives no view of cargo size, weight or handling difficulty.

questions.explanation: Commodity values and volumes reveal the traffic mix but not its physical difficulty. A good answer uses both what the return shows and what it cannot show, such as cargo weight.
questions.hint: Separate price, volume and physical size.

options.misconception: proposes a fix the colony had not used

options.text: By refusing all imports that competed with local production
options.misconception: describes a tariff response rather than financing

options.text: By borrowing from abroad, selling assets, or drawing on the colony's reserves

questions.topic: Concession terms read closely
questions.learningObjective: Apply the conditions stated in a termination clause

stimulus.body: A termination clause allows the government to take over the plant and works if the holder fails to pay the government royalty for two consecutive quarters, and allows the holder to appeal to a commission before any transfer takes place.

questions.stem: Your contract brief reviews the termination clause above. Which reading is correct?

options.text: The government may take the plant at any time it believes the holder is failing
options.misconception: ignores the two quarter and appeal conditions

options.text: The government may act only after two missed quarters and an appeal process
The holder loses the plant automatically as soon as one royalty payment is late
options.misconception: reduces a two quarter trigger to a single late payment

options.text: The clause allows the holder to take over the plant whenever it falls behind
options.misconception: reverses which party holds the remedy

questions.explanation: The clause sets two conditions before any transfer: two consecutive unpaid quarters and an appeal to a commission. A single late payment, or action without the appeal, goes beyond the text.
questions.hint: Count the conditions the clause requires.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Coal smoke and a city's air
questions.learningObjective: Weigh the health and material cost of coal smoke in a city
questions.stem: Your city survey brief asks you to weigh what coal smoke cost a crowded district in health and in damaged property. Draft the assessment.

options.text: The cost was mainly economic, since health effects were not measurable at the time
options.misconception: dismisses the medical complaints of the period

options.text: The cost was mainly medical, since property damage was repaired without charge
options.misconception: invents free repair of soiled property

options.text: Both mattered, with complaints about eyes and lungs alongside ruined washing and paint
The cost was negligible, because soot fell only on roofs nobody occupied
options.misconception: assumes soot fell only on empty property

questions.explanation: Contemporaries complained on both grounds, about breathing and eyes as well as about ruined washing, paint and window frames. A good assessment treats health and material loss as running together.
questions.hint: Read the complaints as they were recorded.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A board of health's mortality return
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a change in a mortality return over time
questions.stem: A board of health's returns show cholera deaths falling from 88 to 21 per year over four years while the parish population grew by 12 percent. What does that change show?

options.text: That the number of cholera cases fell because the parish had fewer inhabitants
options.misconception: invents a shrinking population where there was growth

options.text: That the improvement was caused by the growth in the parish's population
options.misconception: reverses cause and coincidence

options.text: That cholera had been replaced by another fatal disease in the same streets
options.misconception: assumes substitution without any evidence

options.text: That cholera mortality fell per person despite a larger population at risk

questions.explanation: Rates per head fell from 88 to 21 while the population grew, so the improvement is real rather than a shrinking denominator. A growing population would have pushed the rate up.
questions.hint: Divide by the population before judging.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A doctor's note on one street
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a single doctor's report as evidence
questions.stem: Explain to a health committee why a street report alone should not justify building new water works.

answer.exemplar: A good answer sets out what the note does establish, namely a cluster in place and time around a shared supply, and then lists what it cannot establish, such as the organism involved, whether other streets were affected, and how many cases were missed. It concludes that the report should trigger tests and a survey rather than a works scheme on its own.

questions.explanation: A street report shows a pattern worth investigating but not its cause. A good answer names the missing steps, such as confirmation and a wider survey, before any building begins.
questions.hint: Ask what the note cannot rule out.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colonial economy built on one export
questions.learningObjective: Infer a change in labour organisation from employment records

stimulus.body: Plantation employment records for 1892 and 1907 show the permanent wage bill rising from 41,000 to 58,000 pounds while the seasonal workforce fell from 3,900 hands to 2,200. A note records that the price of the export crop fell in three of the five intervening years.

questions.stem: Your labour planning brief cites the employment records above. What does the change in the seasonal workforce suggest?

options.text: That the export crop became more capital-intensive and less labour-hungry per unit
That the colony's population fell, so fewer hands were available to work
options.misconception: explains a labour decline by assuming population loss

options.text: That the government closed the plantations and dismissed the remaining workers
options.misconception: invents a closure that records do not mention

options.text: That wages were cut so sharply that workers left for better paying work
options.misconception: offers a cause the records never record

questions.explanation: A permanent wage bill that rose while seasonal headcount fell suggests fewer transient hands per unit of output, consistent with mechanised handling. The records show no depopulation, closure or wage cut.
questions.hint: Compare the wage bill with the headcount.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A colony's trade return
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cargo manifest matters to harbour design

stimulus.body: A cargo manifest lists outbound consignments as 900 tonnes of raw cotton in compressed bales, 40 tonnes of woven cloth in bales, 210 tonnes of groundnut kernels in sacks, and 120 tonnes of coal in heaped form. Rates for handling are quoted per ton and per bale.

questions.stem: Your stevedoring brief cites the manifest above. Why does the manifest matter to a harbour engineer?

options.text: It shows the total tonnage alone, which is all a stevedoring rate needs
options.misconception: reduces the manifest to a single weight

options.text: It shows that bulk and unitised cargo differ in handling, so one rate will not fit both
It shows the value of the cargo, and therefore the price a wharf can charge
options.misconception: confuses a tonnage manifest with a customs valuation

options.text: It shows which consignments came from the colony and which were transhipped
options.misconception: reads origin information the manifest does not give

questions.explanation: Bales, sacks and heaped coal need different gear, space and rates, and the manifest shows the mix clearly. A ton alone conceals that, and the manifest gives neither cargo value nor origin.
questions.hint: Compare the unit in which each cargo is listed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a cash crop did to land use
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a land use policy that protects food plots at the expense of exports
questions.stem: Your planning brief asks you to evaluate a rule requiring each district to keep a fixed share of its land in food crops. Draft the assessment.

options.text: The rule should be dropped, because food prices always follow world export prices
options.misconception: assumes a fixed price link between two different markets

options.text: The rule should be adopted everywhere, because food plots pay better than export crops
options.misconception: asserts a profitability the brief does not support

options.text: The rule cushions bad harvest years and costs export income when prices are high
The rule is pointless, because districts cannot control what households plant
options.misconception: assumes planting decisions ignore district rules

questions.explanation: A protected share of food land insures against a poor harvest, but takes acreage out of export production exactly when the export price is best. The trade-off is insuring against bad years and giving up good ones.
questions.hint: Ask what the rule gives up in a good year.
